items.title: Writing a sum in sigma notation
items.prose: The series $5 + 9 + 13 + \dots + 41$ has 10 terms. We want to write it as $\sum_{k=1}^{10} f(k)$.
items.question: What is $f(k)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The terms rise by 4, and the first is 5.

byKey.no-start: $4k$ gives 4, 8, ..., 40: one less than each term.
byKey.swap: $k + 4$ rises by 1 each time. These terms rise by 4.
byKey.five: $4k + 5$ gives 9 at $k = 1$. It starts one term too late.

explain.text: The terms rise by 4, so $f(k) = 4k + c$. The first term $4 + c = 5$ gives $c = 1$. Check the last: $4 \times 10 + 1 = 41$.

items.title: A telescoping sum
items.prose: Use $\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)} = \dfrac{1}{k} - \dfrac{1}{k+1}$, which you can check by putting the right side over a common denominator.
items.question: What is $\sum_{k=1}^{99} \dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the first few terms as differences and watch them cancel.

byKey.forever: 1 is the sum to infinity. Stopping at $k = 99$ leaves $-\tfrac{1}{100}$ uncancelled.
byKey.hundred: That is $1 - \tfrac{1}{101}$, the sum up to $k = 100$. The last term here is $\tfrac{1}{99} - \tfrac{1}{100}$.

explain.text: The sum is $(1 - \tfrac12) + (\tfrac12 - \tfrac13) + \dots + (\tfrac{1}{99} - \tfrac{1}{100})$. Every middle fraction cancels, leaving $1 - \tfrac{1}{100} = 0.99$.

items.title: Passing a target
items.prose: Add the terms of $3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + \dots$ one at a time. The sum of the first $n$ terms is $n(2n + 1)$.
items.question: How many terms must you add for the total to pass 1,000 for the first time?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where $n(2n + 1)$ first goes above 1,000.

byKey.terms: You found the term near 1,000. The question is about the running total.

items.title: How long a doubling bet lasts
items.prose: A doubling bettor starts with a £5.00 stake and doubles it after every loss. Their bankroll is £5,000.00, and every stake must be covered by what is left.
items.question: What is the longest losing streak they can pay for in full?

feedback.correct: Nine losses cost $5(2^9 - 1) = 2555$; ten would cost 5,115.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the stakes, not just the last one.

byKey.last-only: The tenth stake, £2,560.00, is below £5,000.00 on its own. But the first nine stakes have already cost £2,555.00, so it cannot be covered.
byKey.divide: You divided £5,000.00 by £5.00. The stakes double, so they use the money up far faster.
byKey.eight: Eight losses cost £1,275.00. A ninth stake of £1,280.00 still fits.

explain.text: After $n$ losses the total staked is $5(2^n - 1)$. Nine losses cost £2,555.00; a tenth stake of £2,560.00 would bring it to £5,115.00. A £5,000.00 bankroll survives 9 losses, and then it is gone.

items.title: Pricing a loan payment
items.prose: A £10,000.00 loan at 0.5% interest a month is repaid by 24 equal monthly payments $P$. The first payment is one month away. The loan is fair when the payments are worth £10,000.00 today.
items.question: What is the monthly payment $P$, to the nearest penny?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The payments' values today form a geometric series with $a = \tfrac{P}{1.005}$ and $r = \tfrac{1}{1.005}$.

byKey.no-interest: £416.67 is £10,000.00 split into 24 parts, with no interest.
byKey.simple: £466.67 adds 0.5% of £10,000.00 for each of 24 months and splits it. Interest falls as the loan is repaid, and is compounded.
byKey.due: That treats the first payment as made today. It comes one month from now.

explain.text: The value today is $P \cdot \tfrac{1 - 1.005^{-24}}{0.005} = 22.5629P$. Setting it to 10,000 gives $P = 443.21$. In all you repay £10,637.04.

items.title: Why a perpetuity is worth c over i
items.prose: A perpetuity pays $c$ at the end of every year, forever, at interest rate $i > 0$. Prove that its value today is $V = \dfrac{c}{i}$, with the shift trick.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $(1+i)V = c + \dfrac{c}{1+i} + \dfrac{c}{(1+i)^2} + \dots$: multiply every term by $1 + i$
$(1+i)V = c + V$: everything after the $c$ is the original series

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $V$ first, then multiply it by $1 + i$.

explain.text: Multiplying by $1 + i$ moves each payment one year closer. The new series is $c$ plus the old one, so $(1 + i)V = c + V$ and $V = \tfrac{c}{i}$. The shift is safe because $\tfrac{1}{1 + i} < 1$, so $V$ is finite.

items.title: Thirty years or forever
items.prompt: Interest is 5% a year. Annuity A pays £1,000.00 at the end of each year for 30 years. Perpetuity B pays £1,000.00 at the end of each year forever. (a) Derive $S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$ by subtracting a shifted copy, justifying each step. (b) Value A today. (c) Explain why B has a finite value, and find it. (d) A colleague says B must be worth far more than A, since it pays forever. Find the difference and explain it.
items.model:
**(a)** Let $S = a + ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{n-1}$, the $n$ terms.

Multiply every term by $r$: $rS = ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{n-1} + ar^n$. Each term moves one place along.

Subtract: every term except $a$ and $ar^n$ appears in both lines, so $S - rS = a - ar^n$.

Factorise: $S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)$. Since $r \ne 1$, divide: $S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$.

**(b)** The payment in year $k$ is worth $\dfrac{1000}{1.05^k}$ today. So $a = \dfrac{1000}{1.05}$, $r = \dfrac{1}{1.05}$ and $n = 30$.

$1 - r = \dfrac{0.05}{1.05}$, so $\dfrac{a}{1 - r} = \dfrac{1000}{0.05} = 20000$.

Then $V_{30} = 20000\,(1 - 1.05^{-30}) = 20000 \times (1 - 0.231377) = \text{£}15{,}372.45$.

**(c)** Here $|r| = \tfrac{1}{1.05} < 1$, so $r^n \to 0$ and the sum to infinity exists: $V_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - r} = \dfrac{1000}{0.05} = \text{£}20{,}000.00$.

**(d)** The perpetuity pays forever, but its extra payments start in year 31. Their value today is $V_\infty - V_{30} = 20000 \times 1.05^{-30} = \text{£}4{,}627.55$: the perpetuity again, discounted 30 years. Each payment is worth $\tfrac{1}{1.05}$ of the one before, so the far future adds less and less. Infinitely many payments, a finite value: the sum converges because $r < 1$. It would be infinite only if $r \ge 1$, that is, with no interest at all.

rubric.text: Writes $S$ and $rS$ and subtracts, saying which terms cancel and why.
Explains that $|r| < 1$ makes $r^n \to 0$ and values B at £20,000.00.
Finds the difference £4,627.55 and explains it as payments from year 31 on, worth B discounted 30 years.
